title: Oil price shocks as IV for inflation on investment

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
- Method: Instrumental Variables (2SLS), using oil price shocks (z) as an instrument for inflation (x) to estimate the causal effect of inflation on corporate investment (y).
- Why IV: Inflation is endogenous to economic activity and firm investment; oil price shocks provide exogenous variation in inflation plausibly unrelated to firm-specific investment shocks, improving identification.
- Key assumptions:
  - Relevance: Cov(z, x | controls) ≠ 0. We will test this via the first-stage F-statistic.
  - Exogeneity/Exclusion: z affects y only through x (no direct effect on investment after conditioning on controls). This is the most debatable assumption here because oil shocks could directly depress investment via costs/demand. We address this with a plausibly exogenous sensitivity analysis (Conley et al. 2012 style) that allows a bounded direct effect of z on y and reports how the inflation effect varies across plausible violations.
  - Linearity and SUTVA: The linear IV model is correctly specified and no interference across firms.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Packages
req_pkgs <- c("AER", "sandwich", "lmtest")
for (p in req_pkgs) {
  if (!requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)) install.packages(p)
}
library(AER)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# 1) Read data
dat <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s24_data.csv")
dat <- na.omit(dat)
cat("Sample size (complete cases):", nrow(dat), "\n")

# 2) Naive OLS (benchmark, not causal)
ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = dat)
ols_rob <- coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1"))
ols_beta <- as.numeric(ols_rob["x", "Estimate"])
ols_se   <- as.numeric(ols_rob["x", "Std. Error"])
ols_p    <- as.numeric(ols_rob["x", "Pr(>|t|)"])
cat("\nNaive OLS estimate (y ~ x + controls):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x = %.4f, SE = %.4f, p = %.4f\n", ols_beta, ols_se, ols_p))

# 3) First stage diagnostics
fs <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = dat)
fs_rob <- coeftest(fs, vcov = vcovHC(fs, type = "HC1"))
fs_beta_z <- as.numeric(fs_rob["z", "Estimate"])
fs_t_z    <- as.numeric(fs_rob["z", "t value"])
fs_F_robust <- fs_t_z^2
cat("\nFirst stage (x ~ z + controls):\n")
cat(sprintf("  coef on z = %.4f, robust t = %.2f, robust F (z) = %.2f\n", fs_beta_z, fs_t_z, fs_F_robust))

# 4) Baseline IV (2SLS): y ~ x + controls | z + controls
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = dat)
iv_rob <- coeftest(iv, vcov = vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1"))
iv_beta <- as.numeric(iv_rob["x", "Estimate"])
iv_se   <- as.numeric(iv_rob["x", "Std. Error"])
iv_p    <- as.numeric(iv_rob["x", "Pr(>|t|)"])

# Also retrieve classical (non-robust) diagnostics incl. weak instrument F
iv_sum <- summary(iv, diagnostics = TRUE)
weakF_classical <- NA
if (!is.null(iv_sum$diagnostics)) {
  # Try to parse the 'Weak instruments' row if present
  diags <- iv_sum$diagnostics
  if ("Weak instruments" %in% rownames(diags)) {
    weakF_classical <- as.numeric(diags["Weak instruments", "statistic"])
  }
}
cat("\nIV (2SLS) estimate (y ~ x + controls | z + controls):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x = %.4f, robust SE = %.4f, robust p = %.4f\n", iv_beta, iv_se, iv_p))
cat(sprintf("  First-stage strength: robust F (from first stage) = %.2f", fs_F_robust))
if (!is.na(weakF_classical)) cat(sprintf(" | classical weak-IV F = %.2f", weakF_classical))
cat("\n")

# 5) Robustness A: IV without controls (just to show sensitivity to controls)
iv_noc <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = dat)
iv_noc_rob <- coeftest(iv_noc, vcov = vcovHC(iv_noc, type = "HC1"))
iv_noc_beta <- as.numeric(iv_noc_rob["x", "Estimate"])
iv_noc_se   <- as.numeric(iv_noc_rob["x", "Std. Error"])
iv_noc_p    <- as.numeric(iv_noc_rob["x", "Pr(>|t|)"])
cat("\nRobustness A — IV without controls (y ~ x | z):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x = %.4f, robust SE = %.4f, robust p = %.4f\n", iv_noc_beta, iv_noc_se, iv_noc_p))

# 6) Robustness B: Plausibly exogenous (Conley-style) sensitivity to a direct effect of z on y
# We assume the direct effect gamma of z on y lies in [gmin, gmax].
# For each gamma, transform y_tilde = y - gamma*z and re-estimate the IV.
gmin <- -0.10  # allows a modest negative direct oil effect on investment (in log points)
gmax <-  0.10  # allows a modest positive direct effect
gstep <- 0.01
ggrid <- seq(gmin, gmax, by = gstep)

beta_grid <- numeric(length(ggrid))
se_grid   <- numeric(length(ggrid))
for (i in seq_along(ggrid)) {
  g <- ggrid[i]
  y_tilde <- dat$y - g * dat$z
  iv_g <- ivreg(y_tilde ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = dat)
  iv_g_rob <- coeftest(iv_g, vcov = vcovHC(iv_g, type = "HC1"))
  beta_grid[i] <- as.numeric(iv_g_rob["x", "Estimate"])
  se_grid[i]   <- as.numeric(iv_g_rob["x", "Std. Error"])
}
beta_min <- min(beta_grid)
beta_max <- max(beta_grid)
uci_min  <- min(beta_grid - 1.96 * se_grid)
uci_max  <- max(beta_grid + 1.96 * se_grid)

cat("\nRobustness B — Plausibly exogenous sensitivity (allowing direct effect of z on y):\n")
cat(sprintf("  Gamma grid: [%.2f, %.2f] step %.2f\n", gmin, gmax, gstep))
cat(sprintf("  Range of 2SLS point estimates for beta_x over gamma grid: [%.4f, %.4f]\n", beta_min, beta_max))
cat(sprintf("  Union 95%% CI over gamma grid: [%.4f, %.4f]\n", uci_min, uci_max))

# 7) Print a concise final result summary
cat("\nSummary:\n")
cat(sprintf("  OLS beta_x = %.4f (SE = %.4f)\n", ols_beta, ols_se))
cat(sprintf("  IV (with controls) beta_x = %.4f (robust SE = %.4f), robust first-stage F = %.2f\n",
            iv_beta, iv_se, fs_F_robust))
cat(sprintf("  Sensitivity (Conley) — beta_x in [%.4f, %.4f] when allowing small direct effects of z\n",
            beta_min, beta_max))
```

## 3. Expected Findings
- Sign: Negative. Higher inflation should reduce real corporate investment by raising uncertainty, distorting price signals, and increasing effective financing costs when nominal frictions bind.
- Magnitude: Modest to moderate. Expect a 2SLS coefficient between roughly -0.05 and -0.20 on log investment per one-unit increase in the inflation measure x (given the scale in the data preview). If x is in percentage points, this implies a small negative elasticity; if x is in decimal units, the semi-elasticity would be larger per unit.
- Sensitivity: If oil prices directly depress investment (violating exclusion), the negative effect of inflation may attenuate toward zero in the plausibly exogenous analysis but should remain negative over small direct-effect ranges if the instrument is reasonably valid.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV/2SLS — oil price instrument; must defend exclusion restriction; test overidentification if multiple instruments
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Inflation reduces investment; exclusion restriction requires sector-level controls
